Indian heritage

Heritage conservation in India: laws, bodies and how it works

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

Heritage conservation in India is shared between the Archaeological Survey of India, which protects monuments of national importance under the AMASR Act 1958, state archaeology departments, city heritage rules, INTACH and other non-government groups, museums, and the communities who use and care for historic places every day.

Talaash Heritage runs workshops on preventive conservation and heritage documentation for colleges, museums and adult learners.

What heritage conservation means

Conservation is the careful management of change. A historic building will weather, crack, flood and be reused whatever anyone does. Conservation tries to slow damage, repair with care, and keep what makes the place significant, while being honest about what is original and what is new.

Good practice rests on a few principles: understand the site before touching it, do as little as necessary, use compatible materials such as lime mortar on old masonry rather than cement, record every intervention, and prefer repairs that can be undone later. Preservation, restoration and reconstruction are different degrees of intervention, and most professionals treat full reconstruction with caution.

The Archaeological Survey of India

The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham and now under the Ministry of Culture, is the main national body. It looks after more than 3,600 centrally protected monuments and sites, from Harappan mounds to colonial buildings, carries out structural and chemical conservation, runs site museums, and regulates excavation across the country. Our guide to the Archaeological Survey of India covers its history and structure.

ASI work is organised in regional circles, each with conservation engineers, archaeologists and chemists. Its science branch deals with problems such as biological growth on stone, salt damage and the yellowing of marble.

The AMASR Act 1958: prohibited and regulated areas

The legal backbone is the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 (AMASR Act). It lets the central government declare monuments and sites of national importance and protects them from damage, unauthorised digging and misuse.

An amendment in 2010 set out clear zones around every centrally protected monument. The first 100 metres from the protected limits is the prohibited area, where new construction is not allowed. The next 200 metres beyond that is the regulated area, where building, repair or renovation needs permission. The same amendment created the National Monuments Authority, which advises on permissions in the regulated area and on heritage bye-laws for individual monuments.

ZoneDistance from protected limitsWhat applies
Protected areaThe monument and its notified boundaryNo alteration without ASI approval
Prohibited areaFirst 100 mNew construction not permitted
Regulated areaFurther 200 m beyond the prohibited areaConstruction or repair needs permission

State departments, cities and INTACH

Most states have their own archaeology departments and ancient monuments acts, protecting thousands of sites of state importance that the ASI does not cover. Some cities, among them Mumbai, have heritage regulations and committees that list historic buildings and precincts and control changes to them.

INTACH, founded in 1984, is a large non-government heritage organisation with chapters across the country. Its chapters list unprotected heritage buildings, run conservation projects, train craftspeople and run heritage education in schools. Universities, museums, private foundations and conservation architects also do a great deal of the practical work.

Movable heritage, such as sculptures, manuscripts and paintings, is protected by the Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, which controls export and requires registration of certain antiquities. Museums handle the day-to-day care, a subject our workshop on preventive conservation introduces.

Communities: the conservation nobody lists

Most of India's heritage is outside any protected list. Village temples, havelis, wells, shrines, sacred groves and old markets survive because families, trusts, priests and neighbourhood groups keep using and repairing them. Living use is often the best protection, though it can also bring unsuitable repairs such as cement plaster or bright enamel paint.

Community archaeology and heritage stewardship try to bring the two worlds together: professionals offer method and records, and local people offer knowledge, care and continuity. Our session on community archaeology and heritage stewardship looks at how this works in practice.

Challenges for heritage conservation in India

Some of these are being met with new tools. Satellite imagery, drones and GIS help map sites and watch for change, as our lecture on remote sensing in archaeology and heritage management explains.

  • Urban growth and construction pressure around protected monuments.
  • Encroachment and unauthorised building inside prohibited areas.
  • Pollution, damp, salts and biological growth damaging stone and plaster.
  • Loss of traditional building skills such as lime work and stone dressing.
  • Illegal trade in antiquities and theft from unguarded temples.
  • Climate change: heavier rain, floods and heat stress on old structures.
  • Limited records for thousands of unprotected buildings.

Heritage conservation notes for students

  • Main national body: Archaeological Survey of India (1861), Ministry of Culture.
  • Key law: AMASR Act 1958, amended 2010.
  • Prohibited area: 100 m from protected limits. Regulated area: a further 200 m.
  • National Monuments Authority: created by the 2010 amendment.
  • Movable heritage: Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972.
  • Non-government body: INTACH (1984).
  • Principles: minimum intervention, compatible materials, reversibility, documentation.

Questions people ask

What is the 100 metre rule around monuments in India?

Under the AMASR Act as amended in 2010, the area within 100 metres of a centrally protected monument's limits is a prohibited area where new construction is not allowed. A further 200 metres beyond that is a regulated area where building or repair needs permission.

What is the role of the ASI in heritage conservation?

The ASI protects and conserves monuments and sites of national importance, carries out structural and chemical conservation, regulates excavations, runs site museums, and enforces the AMASR Act around protected monuments. It works through regional circles across India.

What does INTACH do?

INTACH is a national non-government heritage organisation founded in 1984. It lists unprotected heritage buildings, carries out conservation projects, documents natural and cultural heritage, and runs heritage awareness programmes for schools and the public.

How can students help with heritage conservation?

Students can document local heritage with photographs and notes, record oral histories, join or start a school heritage club, avoid scratching or touching carvings at sites, and report damage to the ASI or state department. Accurate records are useful conservation work.

Which law protects antiquities in India?

The Antiquities and Art Treasures Act, 1972, controls the export of antiquities and art treasures and requires registration of certain categories. Monuments and sites themselves are protected under the AMASR Act 1958 and state monuments acts.
